question: Where and why do real users struggle with this design?

nielsen1993.cite: Nielsen & Landauer (1993). A mathematical model of the finding of usability problems. Proceedings of INTERCHI '93: 206–213.
nielsen1993.checked: quotes read word for word in the vault's text copy (library No. 832) on 20 Nov 2026; page numbers are those printed on the copy (206 onwards); the model's symbols are garbled in the scan, so the formula is given in our words, with the average values from p. 211 and table 1; DOI and pages 206–213 checked against Crossref on 20 Nov 2026

guss2018.cite: Güss (2018). What is going through your mind? Thinking aloud as a method in cross-cultural psychology. Frontiers in Psychology 9: 1292.
guss2018.checked: quotes read word for word in the open-access full text from Europe PMC (PMC6099082, full-text XML) on 20 Nov 2026; places are the article's sections; reference citations are left out

steps.title: Recruit real users
steps.text: Invite people like those who will use the product, not colleagues who built it.

quotes.text: whether test users are representative of the actual user population.
quotes.where: p. 209, factors that change how many problems are found

steps.title: Give real tasks
steps.text: Ask each user to do realistic tasks with the prototype while you watch.

quotes.text: user testing is based on bringing real users in and observing them as they interact with the system in order to perform a given set of tasks

steps.title: Think aloud
steps.text: The user says what goes through their mind as they work, without explaining or analysing it.

quotes.text: Thinking aloud is the concurrent verbalization of thoughts while performing a task
participants are asked to spontaneously report everything that goes through their minds while doing a task, and they are instructed not to interpret or analyze their thinking.

steps.title: Only say “keep talking”
steps.text: When the user falls silent, prompt them to keep talking. Do not ask why: that changes how they think.

quotes.text: An instruction from a facilitator to “keep talking” while the participant performed a task probably would not disrupt the thought process, though an instruction requiring explanation from the participant, like “Tell me why you did this,” would intervene in the cognitive process
quotes.where: section “Reliability and Validity of Thinking-Aloud Protocols”

steps.title: Log the problems
steps.text: Note each place a user stumbles and what they said there. Each new user finds fewer new problems; stop, fix, and test again.

quotes.text: we can expect a Poisson model to describe the finding of usability problems.

expectation.text: Does the act of thinking aloud interfere with and change a person’ cognitive processes while performing the task?
expectation.where: section “Reliability and Validity of Thinking-Aloud Protocols”

exercise.title: How many users are enough?
exercise.intro: Each user finds each problem with some chance λ. Nielsen & Landauer's model gives the share of problems found after n users as 1 − (1 − λ)ⁿ. Move the number of users and λ.
exercise.data_label: Model and values from Nielsen & Landauer (1993): λ averaged 0.31 over their eleven studies (p. 211), and the studies' values in table 1 range from about 0.12 to 0.58. The individual dots are an illustration, drawn with a fixed seed.

limits: The card's defining reference, Ericsson & Simon (1980), has not been read for this page; it is reached through Güss (2018), who reviews it.
Nielsen & Landauer (1993) model both user tests and heuristic evaluations; the exercise applies their average values to user tests, which is a simplification.
